Plasma (physics)

Words: 167 Articles: 2
Physics OurBigBook.com
A plasma is a gas of mobile charged particles whose collective electromagnetic response is important to its dynamics. It commonly contains ions and Electrons, and may also contain a neutral component: complete ionization is not required. A multi-species fluid description has current density J=∑s​qs​ns​us​. The relative motion of the species can matter even when a single-fluid magnetohydrodynamics approximation describes the large-scale dynamics.

Plasma frequency (ωps​=ns​qs2​/(ϵ0​ms​)​)

Words: 54
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
The plasma frequency is the characteristic electrostatic oscillation frequency of a charged species displaced against a neutralizing background. For number density ns​, charge qs​ and mass ms​, the displayed formula uses SI units; in Gaussian units it is ωps​=4πns​qs2​/ms​​. The ion skin depth is c/ωpi​ for the ion species. Different species have different plasma frequencies.

Ion skin depth (di​=c/ωpi​)

Words: 52
Plasma (physics) OurBigBook.com
For a singly charged ion species in Gaussian units, ωpi​=(4πne2/mi​)1/2 is its plasma frequency and di​=cmi​/(4πne2)​. The ion skin depth marks a characteristic scale below which ion and electron motion can separate in a magnetized plasma. Together with the Alfvén speed, it satisfies vA​di​=cB0​/(4πen), the coefficient of guide-field propagation in electron magnetohydrodynamics.

Physical quantity

Physics OurBigBook.com

Dimensionless quantity (dimq=1)

Words: 70
Physical quantity OurBigBook.com
A dimensionless quantity has zero exponent for every base physical dimension. It can be formed by dividing two quantities with the same dimensions, such as x=r/R or q=m/M. Its value is independent of the choice of units for those dimensions. The quantities GM2/R and Lt both have dimensions of energy, so RLt/(GM2) is dimensionless. A dimensionless variable is such a quantity used as an unknown or independent variable in an equation.

Length (L)

Words: 24
Physical quantity OurBigBook.com
Length measures spatial extent or separation. It is a base physical dimension in dimensional analysis, distinguished from the choice of units used to express a particular value.

Philosophy of physics

Words: 285 Articles: 4
Physics OurBigBook.com
Philosophy of physics studies the interpretation and explanatory structure of physical theories, including the relation between mathematical models, observable phenomena and claims about what exists. Its questions include theoretical reduction, emergence and competing formulations of physical locality.

Stochastic Einstein locality

Words: 65
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A formulation of stochastic Einstein locality restricts an event's objective chance to its relevant causal past, rather than spacelike-separated interventions or facts. Different versions constrain either marginal chances or joint conditional probabilities. A one-wing marginal condition alone does not supply outcome independence. To derive a Bell theorem by this route, the proposed locality assumptions must include the appropriate screening-off relation for the two outcomes, together with a common setting-independent past distribution.

Reichenbach common cause principle

Words: 76
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
A classical common-cause explanation seeks past variables which screen off a correlation: conditioned on a sufficiently complete common cause, the correlated events become independent. A Bell local causality model adds local dependence on settings and a single compatible past-variable distribution for all measurement contexts. Providing a different setting-dependent screening variable for each pair of settings does not establish that stronger Bell model. The distinction between a causal mechanism and a purely probabilistic screening construction matters when interpreting this principle.

Emergence

Words: 57
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Emergence concerns novel collective patterns or explanatory structures relative to a lower-level description. Robust effective behaviour can emerge through coarse-graining or singular limits while remaining derivable from the microscopic theory. The stronger claim that genuinely new causal powers cannot be reduced to that theory requires an additional argument; nonanalyticity of a limiting function alone does not establish it.

Theoretical reduction

Words: 55
Philosophy of physics OurBigBook.com
Theoretical reduction relates theories by deriving the laws or predictions of one from another together with explicit identifications of quantities and appropriate domain assumptions. A reduction can require approximation, coarse-graining or a limiting construction. Deduction of an ideal limiting model is different from exact deduction of the same properties for every finite member of a model sequence.

Nuclear physics

Words: 1k Articles: 25
Physics OurBigBook.com
The study of atomic nuclei, their structure, reactions and interactions. Nuclear forces between nucleons and nuclear binding energies connect it to the low-energy consequences of Quantum chromodynamics.

Mössbauer effect

Words: 55
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nucleus bound in a solid can emit or absorb a photon without exciting lattice vibrations, transferring momentum to the solid as a whole. The resulting recoil energy is negligible compared with the isolated-nucleus recoil, making very narrow resonant emission and absorption lines observable. The Pound-Rebka experiment uses this effect to resolve the small frequency shift from gravitational redshift.

Nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE)

Words: 247 Articles: 3
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
At sufficiently high temperature and density, forward and inverse nuclear reactions can balance so that abundances are determined by thermodynamic conditions, nuclear binding and conserved quantities. Silicon burning approaches such an equilibrium among iron-group nuclei. Weak reactions can separately change the electron fraction, so the favored mixture need not be pure iron.

Nickel–iron nuclear equilibrium ratio (n56​/n54​=Knp2​T−3eΔB/(kT))

Words: 91
Nuclear statistical equilibrium OurBigBook.com
Nickel-56 and iron-54 have the same neutron number and differ by two protons. Dividing their nuclear statistical equilibrium abundance formulas cancels the neutron density and leaves the displayed ratio, with ΔB=B56​−B54​ and K containing temperature-independent statistical and mass factors in the simplified model. For material with equal total proton and neutron numbers and only these nuclei plus free protons, charge balance gives np​=2n54​. Thus n56​/n543​∝T−3eΔB/(kT). This has a finite temperature maximum only if the signed energy difference is negative; conventional positive total nuclear binding energies for these two actual isotopes instead give a positive difference.

Electron fraction in stellar matter (Ye​=∑i​Xi​Zi​/Ai​)

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Nuclear statistical equilibrium OurBigBook.com
For electrically neutral fully ionized matter, Ye​ is the number of electrons, or total protons, per baryon. With isotope mass fractions Xi​, charge numbers Zi​ and mass numbers Ai​, the displayed sum neglects small nuclear mass-defect corrections. Strong and electromagnetic reactions preserve it, while electron capture and beta-plus decay reduce it. The proton-to-neutron number ratio is Ye​/(1−Ye​).
Neutron excess (η=1−2Ye​)
Words: 52
Electron fraction in stellar matter OurBigBook.com
The neutron excess is the number of neutrons minus protons per baryon. A mixture of carbon-12 and oxygen-16 has zero neutron excess, while neon-22 contributes 2/22 per baryon in that isotope. Thus a neon-22 mass fraction X22​ gives η=X22​/11. A nonzero excess shifts iron-group ashes from symmetric nickel-56 toward neutron-rich isotopes, even before additional weak reactions occur.

Neutron capture (ZA​X+n⟶ZA+1​X+γ)

Words: 38
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Capture of a neutron increases mass number without immediately changing atomic number. It avoids the charged-particle Coulomb barrier. Subsequent beta-minus decay can increase atomic number. Whether capture is slow or fast compared with relevant beta decays distinguishes the slow neutron-capture process from the rapid neutron-capture process.

Nucleosynthesis

Words: 233 Articles: 4
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Nucleosynthesis is the production of atomic nuclei through nuclear reactions. It includes Big Bang nucleosynthesis, stellar nucleosynthesis and production in explosive or compact-remnant environments. Making nuclei and delivering them to the interstellar medium are separate steps in chemical enrichment.

Stellar nucleosynthesis

Words: 204 Articles: 3
Nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Stellar nucleosynthesis encompasses nuclear production during stellar evolution and explosions, including hydrogen burning, core helium burning, advanced burning and neutron-capture processes. Stellar mass, composition, mixing and mass loss govern which nuclei form and which eventually escape. Slow neutron-capture process and rapid neutron-capture process build many nuclei beyond the iron group.
Neon-22 neutron excess from nitrogen-14 (X22​=1422​X14​,Ye​=21​−14X14​​)
Words: 68
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Two alpha captures and an intervening beta-plus decay turn each nitrogen-14 nucleus into neon-22, incorporating eight baryons from helium and converting one proton to a neutron. With no loss or dilution and nuclear mass defects neglected, a nitrogen-14 mass fraction X14​ therefore yields neon-22 mass fraction (22/14)X14​, not X14​. In otherwise symmetric carbon-oxygen matter this gives the displayed electron fraction in stellar matter. A final neon mass fraction and a pre-helium-burning metallicity must not silently be treated as identical.
Gamma-process nucleosynthesis
Words: 44
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Hot explosive material can use photodisintegration on pre-existing heavy seed nuclei through neutron, proton and alpha emission. This gamma process supplies some proton-rich isotopes that the principal neutron-capture paths bypass. It is a particular mechanism, rather than a synonym for every proposed proton-rich nucleosynthetic process.
r-process (r-process)
Words: 53
Stellar nucleosynthesis OurBigBook.com
At sufficiently large neutron density, successive neutron captures outrun relevant beta decays and produce very neutron-rich nuclei. Decay toward stability afterward yields many heavy isotopes, including some actinides. Neutron-rich ejecta from neutron star mergers provide an established site; particular magnetically driven collapse outflows are additional candidates. This does not imply that every ordinary core-collapse supernova produces a complete heavy-element pattern.

Nuclear reaction

Words: 41
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nuclear reaction transforms one or more atomic nuclei through interactions with particles or other nuclei. Total energy, momentum, electric charge and nucleon number constrain ordinary low-energy reaction bookkeeping. Nuclear fusion, alpha capture, neutron capture and photodisintegration are important examples in stellar nucleosynthesis. Weak processes can also change the proton-to-neutron ratio.

Beta-minus decay (n⟶p+e−+νe​)

Words: 35
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
An energetically allowed weak transition converts a neutron into a proton, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. Free neutron decay is an example; in nuclei, the nuclear binding energy determines whether the transition is possible.

Nuclear fusion (Q=(minitial​−mfinal​)c2)

Words: 131 Articles: 3
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
Fusion combines nuclear reactants into heavier compound nuclei or products. A net decrease in rest mass releases energy; heavier fusion reactions can instead require energy. Stellar nuclear fusion uses exothermic networks to power stars, and quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier permits many charged-particle reactions at stellar temperatures.

Alpha capture (ZA​X+α⟶Z+2A+4​Y+γ)

Words: 58 Articles: 1
Nuclear fusion OurBigBook.com
Capture of an alpha particle increases the mass number by four and atomic number by two. Radiative alpha capture releases a photon, while reactions such as (α,n) can instead emit a neutron. Carbon-12 alpha capture competes with helium production of carbon during core helium burning.
Carbon-12 alpha capture (12C(α,γ)16O)
Words: 20
Alpha capture OurBigBook.com
Capture of an alpha particle by carbon-12 makes oxygen-16. Competition between this reaction and the Triple-alpha process helps determine the carbon-to-oxygen ratio after core helium burning.

Coulomb barrier (V(r)=Z1​Z2​e2/(4πϵ0​r))

Words: 32
Nuclear fusion OurBigBook.com
Repulsion between positively charged nuclei creates this electrostatic energy barrier outside the short-range nuclear interaction. Quantum tunnelling allows reaction at thermal energies below its classical height and contributes the penetration factor in the Gamow peak.

Nuclear photodisintegration (γ+nucleus⟶lighter nuclear products)

Words: 36
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A sufficiently energetic photon can break up a nucleus, consuming energy for an endothermic breakup. In neon burning and silicon burning, such steps combine with captures to form a larger reaction network whose net energy balance can be positive.

Beta-plus decay (ZA​X⟶Z−1A​Y+e++νe​)

Words: 47
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
An energetically allowed weak nuclear transition converts a proton into a neutron, emitting a positron and electron neutrino. Positron annihilation deposits additional electromagnetic energy, while the neutrino can escape. These transitions are steps of the CNO cycle and the pp III branch; an isolated free proton cannot undergo this decay.

Electron capture (ZA​X+e−⟶Z−1A​Y+νe​)

Words: 37
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
A nucleus can capture an electron when energetically allowed, converting a proton into a neutron and emitting an electron neutrino. Beryllium-7 electron capture participates in one of the proton-proton chain branches. Stellar capture rates depend on ionization, mass density and electron phase space.

Nuclear force

Words: 24
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
The residual strong interaction between nucleons. Its long-distance part involves pion exchange and depends on spin and isospin. It is distinct from directly exchanging gluons between color-singlet nucleons.

Atomic nucleus (A=Z+N)

Words: 113 Articles: 3
Nuclear physics OurBigBook.com
The central system of protons and neutrons in an atom. Its mass number A is its baryon number in ordinary nuclear states; Z is the proton number and N the neutron number.

Alpha particle (A=4,Z=2,J=I=0)

Words: 24
Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The helium-four atomic nucleus, containing two protons and two neutrons. Its ground-state spin and isospin are zero. A quantized cubic four-Skyrmion supplies a corresponding nuclear state in the soliton description.

Deuteron (A=2,J=1,I=0)

Words: 23
Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The bound atomic nucleus containing one proton and one neutron. Its ground-state spin is one and its isospin is zero. The appropriately quantized toroidal two-Skyrmion models these quantum numbers.

Nuclear binding energy (Ebind​=(Zmp​+Nmn​−MA​)c2)

Words: 38
Atomic nucleus OurBigBook.com
The positive energy needed to separate a bound atomic nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons. It is the mass defect times c2. In a Skyrmion model of a nucleus, both separated nucleon masses and the multi-soliton state require a consistent quantization and calibration.

Semiconductor

Words: 140 Articles: 3
Physics OurBigBook.com
A semiconductor has an electronic band gap and a conductivity strongly affected by temperature, impurities and carrier injection. Optical absorption can create mobile electrons and holes, enabling a photodiode.

Acceptor impurity

Words: 42
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can accept an electron from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole. A shallow acceptor creates an impurity level in a crystal near and above the valence-band edge. Donor and acceptor levels are descriptions of appropriate dopants, not universal features of every impurity species.

Donor impurity

Words: 43
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
An impurity that can supply an electron to the conduction band. A shallow donor has a localized occupied impurity level in a crystal near and below the conduction-band edge; thermal or other ionization releases its electron. The binding energy depends on the host dielectric response and effective mass.

Mercury cadmium telluride

Words: 28
Semiconductor OurBigBook.com
Mercury cadmium telluride is a semiconductor whose composition tunes its band gap and hence its long-wavelength absorption cutoff. It is widely used as the absorbing material in infrared detector arrays.

Acoustics

Words: 2k Articles: 38
Physics OurBigBook.com

Acoustic eikonal equation in a shear flow ((ω−Ukx​)2=c02​∣k∣2)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Acoustics OurBigBook.com
For a slowly varying parallel shear flow U(y)ex​, the leading WKB method neglects mean-velocity gradients while retaining local advection. The continuity equation and linearized Euler equations then give the displayed acoustic dispersion relation. On the positive intrinsic-frequency branch, ω=Ukx​+c0​∣k∣ and the group velocity is Uex​+c0​k/∣k∣. A wavefront normal is parallel to k; the acoustic energy-ray direction generally differs because of the advection term.

Ray turning in a wall shear layer (ky2​=(ω−Ukx​)2/c02​−kx2​)

Words: 89
Acoustic eikonal equation in a shear flow OurBigBook.com
In a stationary, horizontally homogeneous wall boundary layer, Hamiltonian ray-tracing equations conserve ω and kx​. If U increases away from the wall, downstream-oriented kx​>0 waves have decreasing positive intrinsic frequency and decreasing ky2​. At U=ω/kx​−c0​, the transverse wavenumber vanishes and the acoustic ray turns. For U(0)=0, a downstream launch angle β0​ above the wall can reach a uniform stream of Mach number M∞​ only if cosβ0​≤(1+M∞​)−1. This uses the positive acoustic branch, constant sound speed and no intervening critical layer; a turning point itself requires a uniform local approximation rather than the ordinary WKB method.

Small-height Neumann scattering (∂z​ψ−h′∂x​ψ=0(z=h(x)))

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Acoustics OurBigBook.com
For a rigid rough boundary and incident pressure Aeiαx−iβz, use time dependence e−iωt and α2+β2=k2. The flat reflected wave is Aeiαx+iβz. Expanding the Neumann boundary condition at z=0 gives ∂z​ψ1​=2Aeiαx(β2h+iαh′). For height transform h(q)=∫h(x)e−iqxdx, the outgoing correction is (2A/(2πi))∫(k2−αq)h(q−α)eiqx+iβ(q)z/β(q)dq, with β(q)=k2−q2​ on the outgoing sheet. Controlled height expansions also require adequate slope and spectral regularity; small incident phase displacement alone does not bound every normal-derivative correction.

Oblique coherent reflection from a stationary rigid rough surface (rN​=1−πβ1​∫β(q)(k2−αq)2​Sh​(q−α)dq+⋯)

Words: 75
Small-height Neumann scattering OurBigBook.com
For a zero-mean stationary rough height, the mean first-order correction vanishes. At second order, the boundary derivative is −h∂z2​ψ1​+h′∂x​ψ1​. Averaging this expression using the power spectrum of surface height gives the displayed coherent reflection coefficient. Thus the root mean square height alone does not fix the coherent mean: the height correlation spectrum matters. For roughness varying slowly enough that q≃α in the integral, rN​≃1−2β2σ2. A local random-height phase average needs this additional approximation and is not a general consequence of stationarity.

Sonar

Words: 32
Acoustics OurBigBook.com
Sonar uses sound propagation and reflected signals to detect objects or measure distances. Upward-looking sonar can record sea-ice draft along a moving platform's track; beam width, return selection and processing affect the inferred profile.

Acoustic waveguide

Words: 457 Articles: 5
Acoustics OurBigBook.com
An acoustic waveguide confines sound transversely while allowing longitudinal propagation. Rigid walls impose a homogeneous normal-velocity condition, producing Neumann transverse modes. Each transverse eigenvalue gives a longitudinal wave number: modes below their cutoff decay evanescently, while cut-on modes carry outgoing sound. An open semi-infinite guide can be studied with the Wiener-Hopf method.

Independent-edge radiation from an open planar duct (ϕd​∼−i(−1)nD(r)cos(α/2)sin(θ/2)sin(k0​hsinθ)/(cosθ−cosα))

Words: 109
Acoustic waveguide OurBigBook.com

At leading independent-edge order for large k0​h, the two incident travelling constituents each have amplitude (−1)n/2 at the relevant wall endpoint. Pentaquark OurBigBook.com
Exotic flavour weights can decay into a baryon and a meson while preserving every strong quantum number: uuddsˉ→pK0 or nK+, ddssuˉ→Ξ−π−, and uussdˉ→Ξ0π+. These are quark rearrangements. If above threshold with unsuppressed couplings, such states are short-lived strong resonances. Flavour symmetry alone fixes neither masses nor widths.

Pentaquark OurBigBook.com
Two antisymmetric flavour quark pairs can each transform in 3, combine into 6, and with an antiquark give 6⊗3=10⊕8. The antidecuplet rows are (Y,I)=(2,0),(1,1/2),(0,1),(−1,3/2). Exactly three weights are absent from all three-quark states: (I3​,Y)=(0,2) and (±3/2,−1).
Pauli constraint on three-quark flavour multiplets
Words: 252 Articles: 3
Baryon OurBigBook.com
In a three-quark colour singlet, a symmetric spatial state requires symmetric spin-flavour symmetry. Completely symmetric decuplet flavour couples to symmetric spin 3/2; mixed octet flavour couples to mixed spin 1/2 in the symmetric permutation combination. Antisymmetric singlet flavour cannot have a symmetric S-wave orbital state, since ⋀3C2=0 forbids a completely antisymmetric state of three spin-1/2 quarks. Mixed orbital and spin states can instead realize the required antisymmetry.

Words: 105 Articles: 1
Pauli constraint on three-quark flavour multiplets OurBigBook.com
Two light quarks in a symmetric spatial state and the antisymmetric colour pair inside a three-quark colour singlet require symmetric spin-flavour symmetry. Their isospin singlet and spin singlet are both antisymmetric, while their respective triplets are symmetric. Thus the allowed pairs have (I,Sud​)=(0,0) or (1,1); opposite exchange parities are excluded. Coupling an isospin-zero spin-one-half quark gives an I=0,J=1/2 baryon or I=1,J=1/2,3/2 baryons.

For an isospin singlet quark h of charge qh​, the antisymmetric light-flavour pair gives an I=0,J=1/2 state with charge qh​+1/3. The symmetric light-flavour pairs uu,{ud},dd give I=1 triplets of spins 1/2 and 3/2, with charges qh​+4/3,qh​+1/3,qh​−2/3. These follow from light-diquark spin-isospin correlation and addition of constituent electric charges, with zero orbital angular momentum.

Three light quarks have a six-dimensional single-quark spin-flavour space C3⊗C2. A symmetric spatial ground state and the antisymmetric three-quark colour singlet require the symmetric cube of that space. Its dimension is (38​)=56, and restriction to flavour SU(3) and spin SU(2) gives a baryon decuplet of spin 3/2 and a baryon octet of spin 1/2. The two mixed-permutation multiplicity spaces pair once in the symmetric sector, explaining why the two flavour-octet copies in the unconstrained tensor cube do not represent two distinct ground-state octets.

The invariant colour state of three fundamental quarks is the normalized completely antisymmetric tensor ϵabc​/6​. With this colour factor, the Pauli exclusion principle requires the remaining spatial-spin-flavour wavefunction to be symmetric. Colour and approximate flavour symmetry are distinct SU(3) actions.

Delta baryon OurBigBook.com
Couple the nucleon isospin 1/2 to the pion isospin 1. The highest state ∣3/2,3/2⟩=∣pπ+⟩ is normalized. One application of the total isospin lowering operator gives ∣3/2,1/2⟩=2/3​∣pπ0⟩+1/3​∣nπ+⟩. For a common isospin-invariant two-body decay amplitude, the partial decay rates relative to the Δ++ channel are 2/3 and 1/3. The lowest state gives Δ−→nπ−. Exact relations assume isospin-degenerate masses and common kinematic factors; electromagnetic and quark-mass differences cause corrections.

A population of unstable nuclei with decay constant λ>0 obeys N′=−λN and therefore decays as N(t)=N(0)e−λt.

Radiogenic heating is thermal energy deposited by radioactive decay. If its specific heating rate is Q in watts per kilogram, the volumetric rate is ρQ and the heat input per horizontal area to a column of depth H is ρQH. The distinction between specific and volumetric rates matters in dimensional analysis of a convective heat flux law.

Radioactive decay OurBigBook.com
In a chain N1​→N2​→N3​ with distinct decay constants, the Bateman equation expresses each population as a linear combination of the exponential functions e−λi​t. When two consecutive constants coalesce to λ, the repeated Laplace transform pole produces a term proportional to te−λt.

The Bateman equation gives the populations in a sequential radioactive decay chain. For a parent with population N1​(0) and an initially absent daughter, distinct decay constants give N2​(t)=N1​(0)λ1​(e−λ1​t−e−λ2​t)/(λ2​−λ1​); the first population satisfies N1′​=−λ1​N1​.

For isotropic propagation in three spatial dimensions, a conserved flux from a point source decreases as the reciprocal square of distance. A source of luminosity L produces flux f=L/(4πr2).

A symmetry is a transformation that leaves specified physical laws or observables invariant.

Translational symmetry

Invariance of an action, equation or configuration under a translation. For a continuous spatial translation symmetry, Noether's theorem supplies the conserved momentum; spacetime translation gives the canonical stress-energy tensor.

A discrete symmetry has transformations separated from the identity rather than connected to it by continuously varying symmetry parameters.

A continuous symmetry belongs to a group whose parameters can vary continuously. Spontaneous breaking of such a symmetry can produce Goldstone bosons.

Translation invariance

Translation invariance means that shifting every position by the same constant vector leaves the system unchanged. It prevents an isolated interface or localized solution in a homogeneous infinite domain from having a preferred absolute position.

A wave is a propagating or standing disturbance that can carry energy and momentum. Its oscillations are described by quantities such as wavelength, frequency, and wave speed.

Polarization (waves)

Words: 53 Articles: 1
Wave OurBigBook.com
Polarization of waves describes the direction and time-dependent geometry of the oscillations of a wave. For a transverse wave, linear polarization oscillates along one fixed line; circular polarization rotates along a circle, while elliptical polarization traces an ellipse. Polarization of an electromagnetic wave describes these possibilities for the electric field vector.

Elliptical polarization

Words: 19
Polarization (waves) OurBigBook.com
For an elliptically polarized wave, the displacement vector at a fixed point traces an ellipse during each oscillation period. Linear polarization and circular polarization are limiting cases.

An oscillation is a repeated variation about an equilibrium or central value. A normal mode describes a single frequency of oscillation.

Oscillation OurBigBook.com
Anharmonicity is departure from the motion of a harmonic oscillator, often caused by nonquadratic terms in a potential energy. It can make the oscillation frequency depend on amplitude and generate higher harmonics. A quartic oscillator has one such anharmonic potential energy.

Wave OurBigBook.com
A wave period is the time for a monochromatic wave to complete one oscillation. For angular frequency ω, it is 2π/∣ω∣. In cascade order-of-magnitude estimates the factor 2π is normally suppressed, giving a linear interaction time of order ∣ω∣−1.

Wave OurBigBook.com
The angular spectrum is the transverse Fourier transform of a monochromatic field on a reference plane. In a uniform medium, each transverse wavevector component propagates with a longitudinal wavenumber satisfying the Helmholtz equation. Components beyond the propagating wavenumber range are evanescent waves. The outgoing angular spectrum chooses the longitudinal branch that propagates or decays away from the plane.

Wave amplitude OurBigBook.com
For a scalar complex wave amplitude E, the squared-amplitude scalar wave intensity convention is I=EE∗. It is nonnegative and unchanged by multiplying E by a unit-modulus wave phase factor. This convention is useful in paraxial propagation and phase screen models. Conversion to physical energy flux also depends on the field variable and medium; an arbitrary superposition need not have its full flux determined by this scalar alone. For a random field, ⟨I⟩ is the mean wave intensity, whereas ∣⟨E⟩∣2 is the squared coherent field; these generally differ.

Two sinusoidal signals are in phase quadrature when their phase difference is a quarter cycle, for example cosϕ and sinϕ. Their time averages have zero correlation over a cycle. In a plane wave, this separates fields such as displacement and its time derivative, velocity.

a(x)G(x,y;s)=a(y)G(y,x;s).

Multiplying its frequency-domain equation by a and using the bilinear Green second identity proves the relation. Both Green functions must use the same outgoing or causal prescription. Exchanging source and receiver preserves time lag, and involves no complex conjugation.

Scattered wave (ψs​=ψ−ψi​)

Words: 52
Wave scattering OurBigBook.com
The scattered wave is the part of the total solution produced by the scatterer relative to the prescribed incident wave. It obeys an outgoing radiation condition. For a rough reflecting surface, this convention includes both specular flat-surface reflection and the roughness-dependent correction. Its coherent field is its ensemble mean, which need not equal the full mean intensity.

Incident wave (ψi​)

Words: 47
Wave scattering OurBigBook.com
The incident wave is the prescribed background solution that illuminates a scatterer. It solves the unperturbed Helmholtz equation in scalar time-harmonic models. The scattered contribution is defined by subtracting this field from the total field; reflected waves from a planar boundary are included unless a separate reference reflection is explicitly removed.

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Wave scattering OurBigBook.com
If a unit incident plane wave has scattered field ψs​=eikRf∞​(r,r0​)/R+O(R−2), the differential wave scattering cross-section is
dΩdσ​=∣f∞​(r,r0​)∣2.
(48)
It is the far-field limit of R2 times the scattered-to-incident energy flux ratio. The common physical amplitude normalization cancels when the incident and scattered waves are in the same background medium. The formula assumes that the 1/(4π) Green-function factor, if present, is already included in the far-field pattern.

In the Born approximation for scalar wave scattering, with n=1+μW and zero-mean stationary unit-variance W, define SW​(q)=∫C(s)e−iq⋅sd3s. The leading expectation of the differential cross-section for scalar wave scattering is
⟨σd​⟩=4π2μ2k4​∫C(s)∣V∩(V−s)∣e−iks​⋅sd3s+O(μ3),ks​=k(r−r0​).
(49)
For a regular volume much larger than the covariance range, the overlap is approximately ∣V∣, giving μ2k4∣V∣SW​(ks​)/(4π2). Statistical isotropy, beyond statistical homogeneity, permits the scalar argument ∣ks​∣=2ksin(θ/2). If the spectrum is defined for the index fluctuation rather than W, it already contains μ2.

Uncentered wave-field correlation (C(r,r′)=E[E(r)E(r′)∗])
Words: 62
Wave propagation in a random medium OurBigBook.com
For a complex random wave amplitude, this two-point expectation retains the coherent field and uses a complex conjugate on the second amplitude. It is not a normalized wave-field correlation coefficient. Subtracting E[E(r)]E[E(r′)]∗ gives the centered covariance function. At coincident points the uncentered wave-field correlation equals the mean wave intensity. Under second-order stationarity it depends only on the separation and has a spectral measure of a stationary random field. A deterministic field is included by taking a degenerate ensemble.
Ensemble-averaged wave intensity (E[∣E∣2]=∣E[E]∣2+E[∣E−E[E]∣2])
Words: 71
Wave propagation in a random medium OurBigBook.com
For a random complex wave amplitude E, its mean squared amplitude is I=E[∣E∣2]. Expanding E=m+(E−m), with m=E[E], gives
E[∣E∣2]=∣m∣2+E[∣E−m∣2].
(50)
The mixed terms vanish. Thus the squared coherent field is only one part of the mean intensity; the other is the diffuse contribution. A fixed acoustic or optical normalization converts this squared-amplitude quantity to physical energy flux. This ensemble mean differs from the angularly averaged radiative-transfer mean intensity.
Coherent wave field (m=E[E])
Words: 313 Articles: 3
Wave propagation in a random medium OurBigBook.com
In wave propagation in a random medium, the coherent field is the expectation of the complex wave amplitude, m(r)=E[E(r)]. The remaining field E−m has zero expectation. This is the coherent and diffuse wave fields decomposition. Statistical homogeneity of the medium does not make m spatially constant when the incident field is localized: translation symmetry applies to the response together with its incident data. The coherent component can attenuate while the total ensemble-averaged wave intensity remains substantial.
Gaussian coherent-field propagation in the Markov approximation (m=e−γ(x−x0​)Efree​)
Words: 71
Coherent wave field OurBigBook.com
For the linear weak-index parabolic wave equation, a Markov approximation with integrated covariance B(η)=∫R​C(s,η)ds gives
mx​=2ki​mzz​−γm,γ=2k2μ2B(0)​.
(51)
The drift follows by converting the multiplicative Stratonovich integral ikμE∘dB to an Itô integral for a Brownian field with transverse covariance B. For a Gaussian beam with one transverse coordinate entering the random region at x0​, m(x,z)=e−γ(x−x0​)Efree​(x,z). The coherent field retains transverse beam structure. The white-noise closure needs short longitudinal correlations and the corresponding separation of propagation scales; Gaussian one-point statistics alone are insufficient.
Weak-fluctuation memory equation for the coherent field
Words: 178 Articles: 1
Coherent wave field OurBigBook.com
For a parabolic wave equation with n=1+μW, a zero-mean stationary real field W of unit variance, and L0​=i∂z2​/(2k), finite-correlation perturbation theory gives
mx​​=L0​m+2ikμ2​m−k2μ2∫x0​x​∫R​C(x−s,z−ζ)Gx−s​(z−ζ)m(s,ζ)dζds+O(μ3).​
(52)
Here m is the coherent field, C is the autocorrelation function of a random field and G is the one-coordinate Fresnel propagator. Expand the random solution once using the Duhamel principle, multiply by W and average to obtain the memory term. The local phase term comes from the μ2W2 term in n2. The expansion is for fixed propagation distances with suitable covariance regularity and moment bounds. A Markov approximation is an additional scale assumption that can turn this integral equation into a local attenuation equation.

Words: 76
Weak-fluctuation memory equation for the coherent field OurBigBook.com
If the physical refractive index is n=1+μW, then n2−1=2μW+μ2W2. In the parabolic wave equation, the last term produces ikμ2E[W2E]/2 in the mean equation. For unit-variance, finite-correlation fluctuations, E[W2E]=m+O(μ) in a weak-fluctuation expansion, giving a coherent phase drift ikμ2m/2 to second order. This term is absent if the model deliberately linearizes n2−1 to 2μW. It is not obtained by squaring ideal Gaussian white noise, whose pointwise square is not the finite-variance random variable W2.

The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency of a wave when source and observer move relative to one another. For light and a small radial recession speed vr​≪c, Δλ/λ≃vr​/c, where λ is wavelength. This is the basis of Doppler spectroscopy.

The Lorentz transformation changes the photon four-momentum and therefore its frequency, producing the displayed formula for a boost along the first axis. A kinematic redshift is the relativistic Doppler effect from relative motion of emitter and receiver. With positive radial recession speed v, its small-velocity limit is zkin​=v/c+O(v2/c2). A peculiar velocity gives such a factor in addition to cosmological redshift.
